vignette:
Gerald Whitmore is a 72-year-old single software engineer who presented for his initial intake carrying a worn canvas bag and sitting with his back to the wall, his eyes moving steadily across the faces of everyone in the waiting room before he would agree to follow the intake coordinator down the hall. He explained this without embarrassment, as though it were simply practical. It was only after several sessions that the fuller story began to emerge.

Roughly eighteen months ago, Gerald was traveling abroad for a consulting project when he was detained by local authorities under circumstances that remain legally unresolved. Over the course of several days, he was held in an isolated room, subjected to prolonged sleep deprivation, physical coercion, and what he describes with careful understatement as "interviews that went beyond questioning." At various points, men entered the room whose faces he could not read - whose expressions remained flat and unreadable regardless of what was happening - and he learned, over those days, to study every microshift in their features for information about what was coming next. His captors sometimes left without doing anything; sometimes they did not. The difference, he came to understand, was encoded somewhere in how they held themselves, in the set of a jaw or the angle of a shoulder. Reading that difference felt like survival. The room had a heavy door. He could hear it being locked from the outside each time they left. That sound - the mechanical finality of it - became the boundary of his world.

He was eventually released and returned to the United States, and for the first several weeks he told himself he was recovering normally. He went back to his apartment, back to his workstation, back to the rhythmic logic of code. But the symptoms that had seemed like reasonable responses to an extraordinary situation did not recede. At night he found he could not settle into sleep; some part of him remained convinced that lowering his guard was not safe, and he would lie awake listening to the building. He began checking the locks on his front door before bed - once, then twice, then in a circuit that could take twenty minutes. He told himself this was reasonable. He lives alone, after all.

What he found harder to explain, even to himself, was what happened at work. Gerald's job, now conducted entirely remotely, requires long hours at a screen in his home office, and the solitude that had once felt comfortable now pressed on him in ways he struggled to articulate. He had come to believe, with a quiet but persistent certainty, that being alone in a room left him exposed in some way he could not fully name, and he began leaving the door to his office open, then moving his laptop to the kitchen where the ambient noise of the street provided some reassurance. He started scheduling unnecessary video calls - not because he wanted to talk, but because having another face on the screen made the space feel less dangerous. His productivity declined. A project deadline was missed. His supervisor, who had known him for years, asked if everything was all right, and Gerald said that it was.

He had also, by this point, largely stopped reaching out to the few friends he had maintained over the years. He had lost something he could not quite name - some basic assumption that other people were trustworthy, that the world operated according to recognizable rules. He felt set apart from people who had not experienced what he had, and he found he could not locate the words that would bridge that distance. At the same time, he was working hard, in a way that exhausted him, to keep certain thoughts from forming fully - pushing away anything that moved toward the room, the door, the faces. He had begun to worry, in quieter moments, that the effort required to do this was itself a sign that something in him had broken permanently, and he monitored his own thinking with a vigilance that left him depleted by midday.

What finally brought him to seek help was a conversation with his sister, who told him plainly that he seemed like a different person. He had dismissed it at the time. But the words stayed with him, because he was afraid she was right - and because the man he had been before felt, to him, like someone worth trying to recover.
